source: International Monetary Fund, International Reserves and Foreign Currency Liquidity (IRFCL), official reserve assets (IRFCLDT1_IRFCL65_USD), monetary authorities and central government (S1XS1311), monthly, US dollars
note: Each row is a country's official reserve assets at the end of the month, as it reports them to the IMF, in US dollars: foreign currency reserves, gold, special drawing rights, its position at the IMF and other reserve assets. Countries value gold differently, and the United States and Saudi Arabia use an official price of about $42 an ounce, so their rows are far below what their gold is worth; official gold at one market price has its own book. The euro area's total is left out because its central banks have their own rows, and Taiwan does not report to the IMF. This is not the IMF's currency split of the world's reserves, which covers foreign currency only. A country that reports later than the others keeps its last figure for up to six months, and its row says which month (at the latest month: Armenia (Jun 2026), Cambodia (Feb 2026), Croatia (Jun 2026), Egypt (May 2026), Estonia (Jun 2026), France (Jun 2026), Guatemala (Jun 2026), Kosovo (Jun 2026), Morocco (Jun 2026), Nicaragua (May 2026), Norway (Jun 2026), Paraguay (Mar 2026), Rwanda (Jun 2026), Thailand (Jun 2026), West Bank and Gaza (Mar 2026)). Left out because their latest figure is older than that: Bolivia, Jamaica, Kyrgyz Republic, Namibia, Slovakia, Tunisia. The book ends at the latest month in which the countries that had actually reported hold at least nine tenths of the money, so a month where most figures would be carried is not shown yet. It starts in the first month in which the countries reporting by then hold at least 99 in every 100 dollars of today's reserves; the rest start later and are blank before their first figure, so the total steps up a little when each joins: Sri Lanka (Oct 2015), Cambodia (Jan 2016), Serbia (May 2017), Mongolia (Dec 2017), Paraguay (Oct 2018), Ecuador (Dec 2018), Bosnia and Herzegovina (Jul 2019), Angola (Oct 2020), Panama (Jul 2021), Botswana (Mar 2022), Rwanda (Apr 2022), Kosovo (Nov 2022). The total is our sum of the rows with a figure that month. Source: International Monetary Fund.
